p: Born on 23 September 1748, Asaf-ud-Daula was the son of Shuja-ud-Daula and of Umat-ul-Zohra, better known as Bahu Begum. He became nawab at the age of 26 on his father's death in January 1775, with the aid of the British East India Company. His younger brother Saadat Ali led a mutiny in the army, which the British Colonel John Parker defeated decisively. Asaf's first chief minister, Mukhtar-ud-Daula, was assassinated in the revolt. His position as Nawab wazir was ratified by the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II.

After the revolt he restructured the government, appointing nobles favourable to him and British officers to his army. Hasan Riza Khan became chief minister, ably assisted by Haydar Beg Khan, and Tikayt Ray finance minister. His mother remained a challenge to his rule: she controlled much of the treasury, held her own jagirs and armed forces, and at one point sought the Company's help in appointing ministers opposed to him.

Shuja-ud-Daula had left two million pounds sterling in the vaults of the zenana, which his widow and his mother claimed under a will that was never produced. When Warren Hastings pressed the nawab for the debt due to the Company, Asaf obtained from his mother a loan of 26 lakh rupees against a jagir of four times the value, and later 30 lakh more in return for a full acquittal and the Company's recognition of her jagirs for life. The jagirs were afterwards confiscated on the ground of her complicity in the rising of Chait Singh.

The Bara Imambara, or Asafi Imambara, was begun as a charitable project to give employment in the famine of 1784, in which even nobles were reduced to penury. It is said that over 20,000 people worked on it, and that nobles were paid to pull down part of the work in secret at night so that their dignity was kept. The Rumi Darwaza, sixty feet tall, was modelled in 1784 on the Sublime Porte in Istanbul.

He died in Lucknow on 21 September 1797 and is buried at the Bara Imambara. A saying still known in the city records his generosity: to whom even God does not give, Asaf-ud-Daula gives. The painter Johann Zoffany portrayed him several times, and the Urdu poet Mir Taqi Mir was at his court.

notes: The article gives his rule as beginning 26 January 1775 in the lede and his father's death as 28 January 1775 in the body; I wrote 'January 1775'.
The article spells the name Asaf-ud-Daula / -Dowlah / -Doula; I kept the entry's spelling.
Mir Taqi Mir is named only in the article's See also list ('Urdu poet at the Lucknow court of Asaf-ud-Daula').
The construction stories are given with 'It is said', as in the article.
